body_markdown:
## What


Defines


an


Effective Cyber Resilience Strategy


?


Cyber resilience is a broader concept than considering backup, disaster recovery, or incident response separately. NIST defines cyber resiliency as the ability to “anticipate, withstand, recover from, and adapt to” adverse conditions affecting cyber-enabled systems. That definition matters because it places recovery inside a continuous operating cycle rather than at the end of an emergency plan.


An effective strategy should begin with business services and impact tolerances. Leaders should identify the minimum set of capabilities required to keep the organization functioning, then trace the applications, identity services, infrastructure, and data those capabilities depend on. This service-centered view prevents a common failure: restoring technically available systems in an order that does not restore a usable business process.


A mature strategy also distinguishes


[cyber resilience](https://www.commvault.com/cyber-resilience) from availability. High availability can keep a service running through routine


component


failure, while resilience assumes that systems, credentials, or data may be actively compromised. That distinction changes architecture, decision rights, and the evidence


required


before restoration.


Ownership should also cross organizational boundaries. Security teams may detect and contain an attack, infrastructure teams may rebuild environments, application owners may validate functionality, and business leaders may decide what level of degraded service is acceptable. The strategy should define who makes each decision, what evidence they need, and how authority changes during crisis operations.


Commvault


’


s


[R esOps (r esilience o peration s)](https://www.commvault.com/explore/resilience-operations) approach


helps support


this need by aligning operations, security, and infrastructure teams around critical services, measurable recovery targets, and continuous validation.


Resilience objectives should also be specific enough to guide investment. A stated goal to recover quickly offers little direction; a defined service target, dependency map, and validation standard reveal which improvements will change the outcome.


The output should be a prioritized resilience backlog, not a static policy. Gaps such as undocumented dependencies, untested identity recovery, or unclear data validation criteria should be assigned owners and deadlines.


Progress can then be measured through recovery test results, unresolved risks, and the organization’s ability to meet defined impact tolerances. That turns cyber resilience from an aspiration into an operating discipline that can improve as systems and threats change.
